title: Δειλὸς κυνηγὸς καὶ δρυτόμος
titleEn: The Cowardly Hunter and the Woodcutter
part: The Cowardly Hunter and the Woodcutter (Chambry 93 · Perry 326)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 93 (= Perry 326). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », [ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λέοντός τις κυνηγὸς ἴχνη ἐπεζήτει· δρυτόμον δὲ ἐρωτήσας εἰ εἶδεν ἴχνη λέοντος καὶ ποῦ κοιτάζει, ἔφη· « Καὶ αὐτὸν τὸν λέοντά σοι ἤδη δείξω. »
sentences.tr: Leontos tis kynēgos ichnē epezētei· drytomon de erōtēsas ei eiden ichnē leontos kai pou koitazei, ephē· « Kai auton ton leonta soi ēdē deixō. »
sentences.l: A certain hunter was searching out the tracks of a lion; and having asked a woodcutter whether he had seen a lion's tracks and where it beds down, he said: « Even the lion himself I will show you at once. »
sentences.i: A hunter was searching out a lion's tracks; and when he had asked a woodcutter whether he had seen a lion's tracks and where the beast lay up, the woodcutter answered: « I will show you the lion himself, and at once. »
sentences.n: The subject changes without warning at ἔφη: the asking belongs to the hunter, the answer to the woodcutter, and Greek leaves the reader to supply the shift. ἐρωτήσας εἰ introduces an indirect question whose verbs keep the tense of the words actually spoken (εἶδεν, κοιτάζει). καί before αὐτὸν τὸν λέοντα is 'even, the lion himself' — he offers more than was asked for.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ὠχριάσας ἐκ τοῦ φόβου καὶ τοὺς ὀδόντας συγκρούων εἶπεν· « Ἴχνη μόνα ζητῶ, οὐχὶ αὐτὸν τὸν λέοντα. »
sentences.tr: Ho de ōchriasas ek tou phobou kai tous odontas synkrouōn eipen· « Ichnē mona zētō, ouchi auton ton leonta. »
sentences.l: But he, having gone pale from fear and knocking his teeth together, said: « I am looking for tracks only, not the lion himself. »
sentences.i: But the hunter turned pale with fear and, his teeth chattering, said: « It is tracks only that I am looking for, not the lion himself. »
sentences.n: ὠχριάω is to turn ὠχρός, pale-yellow. συγκρούω is 'to knock together', and the present participle keeps it running while he speaks: his teeth chatter. οὐχί is the emphatic form of οὐ.

sentences.t: [Ὅτι] τοὺς θρασεῖς καὶ δειλοὺς ὁ μῦθος ἐλέγχει, τοὺς τολμηροὺς ἐν τοῖς λόγοις καὶ οὐκ ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις.
sentences.tr: [Hoti] tous thraseis kai deilous ho mythos elenchei, tous tolmērous en tois logois kai ouk en tois ergois.
sentences.l: [That] the fable exposes the rash and cowardly, those daring in words and not in deeds.
sentences.i: The fable exposes the rash and cowardly — men daring in what they say and not in what they do.
sentences.n: Chambry brackets Ὅτι as an interpolation, and the brackets mean he deletes it: the sentence already carries its own governing verb in ἐλέγχει, so the subordinator has nothing to hang on. ἐλέγχω is to put to the test and so to show up, to convict. A single article τούς covers both θρασεῖς and δειλούς — they are one set of men, not two — and the phrase in apposition says which: rash with the tongue, a coward with the hands.
